entries.clue: A letter is lenient (10)

blocks.note: 'a' = per, as in 'ten pounds a head'
a missive is a letter

annotation.surface: Someone decides that a single letter of the alphabet is soft on others.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like an alphabet character, but here it is the kind you post: a missive.
annotation.definitionFit: Permissive and lenient both describe someone who allows a lot and punishes little.

entries.clue: Ring? Strip (you made out) (4)

indicatorNotes.you made out: what you 'made out' is what you caught by ear, not the spelling

blocks.note: to peel is to strip; say it and listen rather than spell it

annotation.surface: A terse note: someone is told to strip, and the aside suggests they already got the message.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Made out' can mean kissed or managed, but here it means 'heard, discerned'.
annotation.definitionFit: A peal is the ringing of a set of bells.

entries.clue: Where one inevitably ends up emulating the locals? (4)

annotation.definition: Where one inevitably ends up emulating the locals

blocks.note: the proverb that all roads lead there: wherever you set out, this is the destination
the proverb about doing as its citizens do once you arrive

annotation.surface: A wry observation about travellers who go native.
annotation.walkthrough: Two proverbs meet: all roads lead to Rome, so you inevitably end up there, and when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
annotation.definitionFit: Rome is the city both sayings are about.

entries.clue: Part of religious group, saint prays for means of repelling creepy-crawlies (6,6)

blocks.note: part of a sect is IN SECT
S = saint
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A saint belonging to some religious order prays to be spared the bugs.
annotation.walkthrough: The word breaks fall in different places in the wordplay and the answer, which is what hides it: the religious group and the praying saint turn into bug killers.
annotation.definitionFit: Insect sprays are aerosols used to drive off or kill bugs.

entries.clue: Some laceless items, podalically oriented – not starchy, principally? (4-3)

annotation.definition: Some laceless items, podalically oriented – not starchy, principally?

indicatorNotes.principally: principally = in the first place, so take each word's first letter

blocks.clueFragment: Some laceless items, podalically oriented – not starchy
blocks.note: first letters of Some Laceless Items Podalically Oriented Not Starchy

annotation.surface: A pompous description of relaxed, unfussy footwear.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and a description of the shoes: casual, lace-free footwear that is 'not starchy'. 'Podalically' means to do with the feet.
annotation.definitionFit: Slip-ons are shoes without laces that you slide your feet into.

entries.clue: Nondescript vehicle Everyman will advocate at the outset (7)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: the outset of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a van is a vehicle
the setter speaking: 'I will' = I'LL
first letter of advocate

annotation.surface: The setter promises to recommend some dull car before anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by name, so 'Everyman will' means 'I will', shortened to I'LL.
annotation.definitionFit: Vanilla, as in plain ice cream, means ordinary and lacking special features.

entries.clue: Biblical character in thesaurus (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the next word

blocks.note: thESAUrus

annotation.surface: Looking up a figure from the Bible in a book of synonyms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a letter, but it is a person: Esau, Jacob's twin brother.
annotation.definitionFit: Esau is the elder son of Isaac in Genesis.

entries.clue: Nestle with William’s feathered friends (10)

blocks.note: to spoon is to cuddle up
Bill is short for William, so William's = BILL'S

annotation.surface: Someone snuggles up with William's pet birds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feathered friends' is a jokey stock phrase for birds.
annotation.definitionFit: Spoonbills are wading birds with flat, spoon-shaped bills.

entries.clue: I see below rose (10)

blocks.note: under = below
rose = stood (up), past tense

annotation.surface: Someone spots a flower growing beneath them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the flower but is the past tense of rise.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Understood!' and 'I see' are both replies meaning you have grasped something.

entries.clue: University department in which things may be granted? (10)

blocks.note: the office that decides which applicants get a place
points conceded in an argument, as in 'granted, you have a point'

annotation.surface: A university office where places or grants are handed out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Granted' in the second sense means conceded, as in 'granted, I was wrong'; admissions are things you concede.
annotation.definitionFit: The admissions office decides who gets in, and an admission is something you grant is true.

entries.clue: Atmosphere – ruination – that’s regressive (4)

indicatorNotes.that’s regressive: regressive = going backwards, so the word is written back to front

blocks.note: doom = ruin

annotation.surface: A gloomy remark that the prevailing feeling of doom is a step backwards.
annotation.walkthrough: The dashes make it read as a list of gloomy nouns; only the last phrase is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the feeling that hangs over a room or a crowd.

entries.clue: Like attractive accounts when entire thigh’s displayed (4-8)

indicatorNotes.displayed: to display is to spread out, so the letters are laid out anew

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A saucy suggestion that something draws attention when a whole thigh is on show.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is racy; the answer is banking: a high-interest savings account is the attractive one.
annotation.definitionFit: Savings accounts paying high interest are the ones customers find appealing.

entries.clue: Food for the young fish initially diving deep (6,6)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: a school is a group of fish
first letter of diving
deep = inner, as in deep-seated or inner feelings

annotation.surface: Young fish get their meal by diving to the depths.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Food for the young fish' reads as one phrase; the definition stops at 'young', and 'fish' starts the wordplay as a school.
annotation.definitionFit: A school dinner is the midday meal served to pupils at school.

entries.clue: A Samaritan adrift in Atlantic ship (5,5)

indicatorNotes.adrift: adrift = loose and wandering, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A good Samaritan lost at sea on a transatlantic vessel.
annotation.walkthrough: The Santa Maria was Columbus's flagship on his 1492 Atlantic crossing.
annotation.definitionFit: The Santa Maria is the most famous ship to have crossed the Atlantic.

entries.clue: Alluring security measure that keeps paper in place (7,3)

blocks.note: alluring = drawing (in), attracting
a PIN is the personal number protecting a bank card

annotation.surface: An attractive-sounding security feature for holding documents down.
annotation.walkthrough: A drawing pin is the British name for a thumbtack. The definition is a relative clause, standing for 'thing that keeps paper in place'.
annotation.definitionFit: A drawing pin is pushed into a board to hold a sheet of paper.
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a relative clause, 'something that keeps paper in place'

entries.clue: Seizes chair’s comfortable features (not masculine) (7)

blocks.note: armrests make a chair comfortable
M = masculine, removed

annotation.surface: Someone grabs the cosy parts of a chair.
annotation.walkthrough: ARMRESTS loses its M to give ARRESTS.
annotation.definitionFit: To arrest someone is to seize them.

entries.clue: I refuse to believe in a model bank robbery (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition speaks as the answer: an atheist would say 'I refuse to believe'

blocks.note: used as it stands
the Model T, Ford's famous car
a heist is a robbery

annotation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of a textbook bank job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I refuse to believe in' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is only a link; the definition is the atheist's own statement.
annotation.definitionFit: An atheist is someone who refuses to believe in God.

entries.clue: Blocks two-thirds of the toady protuberances (7)

indicatorNotes.two-thirds of: keep two of the three letters of THE

blocks.note: the first two letters of THE
toads are proverbially warty

annotation.surface: Something obstructs the bumps on a toad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Toady' looks like a flatterer but means toad-like, and toads are famous for warts.
annotation.definitionFit: To thwart is to block or frustrate.

entries.clue: Doorman who might give you hell? (2,5)

annotation.definition: Doorman who might give you hell

blocks.note: the surface wants a nightclub bouncer; the setter means the keeper of heaven's gate
the surface hears a telling-off; the setter means refusing entry and sending you down

annotation.surface: A bouncer who might give you a hard time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Give you hell' sounds like a telling-off, but it is literal: St Peter guards heaven's gates and may send you the other way.
annotation.definitionFit: St Peter is traditionally the keeper of the gates of heaven.

entries.clue: Trembling, drool about new American football star (7)

indicatorNotes.Trembling: trembling = shaking, so the letters of drool are shaken up
indicatorNotes.about: about = around, so the shaken word goes around the other letters

blocks.note: anagram of drool
N = new
A = American

annotation.surface: A trembling, drooling fan gushes over a new US sporting hero.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American football' reads as one phrase, but 'American' belongs to the wordplay and the star plays soccer.
annotation.definitionFit: Ronaldo is the name of more than one famous footballer, notably Cristiano Ronaldo.

entries.clue: Shabby slate (3-4)

blocks.note: worn and neglected, as a building left without repairs
British informal: to criticise harshly, as a critic slates a play

annotation.walkthrough: 'Slate' looks like a roofing tile, which fits the shabby-building picture, but it is a verb. The hyphen blurs the adjective and the two-word verb.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective describes decay; the phrasal verb means to disparage, a sense British critics use constantly.

entries.clue: What makes … what makes the world go round … go round? (5-7)

annotation.definition: What makes … what makes the world go round … go round

blocks.clueFragment: what makes the world go round
blocks.note: the saying's answer: cash, the thing everything runs on
…go round: whatever sets something turning, a top or a wheel

annotation.surface: A riddle nesting one question inside another.
annotation.walkthrough: The saying goes that money makes the world go round; a spinner makes things go round, so a spinner of money is a money-spinner.
annotation.definitionFit: A money-spinner is something that earns a lot of money.

entries.clue: Take public transport up to find shopping centre (4)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom

blocks.note: surface padding: it makes the instruction read naturally
a tram is a form of public transport

annotation.surface: Advice to ride the bus or tram into town for the shops.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up' reads as travelling up to town, but in a down entry it sends the letters upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A somewhat dated word for a market or trading place, surviving in names like K-Mart.

entries.clue: Gemstone? It’s love, mate (4)

blocks.note: love = nil in tennis, the shape of O
a pal is a mate

annotation.surface: Someone explains that a jewel is a token of affection to a friend.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love, mate' sounds like a chatty address, but splits into two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the milky, rainbow-flecked stone is one of the precious gems.

entries.clue: Gripped in booby trap (4)

indicatorNotes.booby: a booby is a fool, so 'booby trap' is a foolishly arranged TRAP

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: Someone caught fast in a hidden snare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Booby trap' is a stock phrase, so 'booby' passes as part of it rather than the signal to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Rapt means completely gripped or absorbed.

entries.clue: More than one character in finest robe lampooned, being flash here (6,4)

indicatorNotes.More than one character in: several letters found inside the following words

blocks.note: fineSTROBELAMPooned

annotation.surface: Someone mocked for a flashy outfit in the finest robe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lampooned' looks like an anagram signal, but the answer simply runs through the words. 'Flash' is literal: a strobe lamp flashes.
annotation.definitionFit: A strobe lamp gives rapid flashes of light.
annotation.definitionNote: the definition is descriptive: the thing that is flashing here

entries.clue: Complaint heard in E. London, somewhere in E. London (4)

indicatorNotes.heard in E. London: as spoken in a Cockney accent, which drops the H

blocks.note: Hackney without its H

annotation.surface: A grumble overheard in the East End about somewhere in the East End.
annotation.walkthrough: Hackney is a borough of East London, and the Cockney accent of East London drops the H, leaving 'Ackney.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Complaint' in its medical sense, an ailment; spots on the skin qualify.

entries.clue: A monkey and 20 ponies? (5,5)

blocks.note: not the animal: British slang for five hundred pounds
not horses: a pony is slang for twenty-five pounds, so twenty make another five hundred

annotation.surface: An odd inventory from a zoo or a farm.
annotation.walkthrough: British money slang: a monkey is £500 and a pony £25, so 20 ponies is another £500, and the sum is a grand (£1,000).
annotation.definitionFit: Adding the two amounts gives a total of a grand.
